text:
Apollo 13: The Successful Failure

On April 11, 1970, at 2:13 in the afternoon Houston time, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Cape Kennedy carrying James Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise toward the Moon. It was the seventh crewed mission in the Apollo program and the third intended lunar landing. Americans had already seen two crews walk on the Moon, and the public had begun to treat the flights as routine. Television networks had declined to broadcast the crew's early transmissions. That would change within three days.

Lovell, the commander, was the most experienced spaceflyer alive, a veteran of Gemini 7, Gemini 12 and Apollo 8. Haise was a rookie who would pilot the lunar module, named Aquarius. Swigert, the command module pilot, had joined only days earlier. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been grounded when he was exposed to German measles, and Swigert stepped in on short notice. The command module was called Odyssey. The plan was to land at the Fra Mauro highlands, a hilly region that scientists wanted to sample.

The launch was not flawless. The center engine of the second stage shut down early, and the others burned longer to compensate, but the spacecraft reached orbit and then set out for the Moon. For two days the flight was uneventful. The crew transmitted a television broadcast on the evening of April 13, showing viewers around the spacecraft. Few paid attention. Moments after it ended, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, a routine task that prevented the supercooled contents from settling.

Swigert flipped the switch at about 9:07 p.m. Houston time. Fifty-six hours into the flight, and roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, there was a loud bang. The cause lay in oxygen tank number two. Years earlier, a thermostat in the tank had been damaged during ground testing, and the insulation on its wiring had been scorched during a long pre-launch heating cycle. When the fans were switched on, a spark ignited the exposed wires inside the tank filled with liquid oxygen. Pressure rose, the tank ruptured, and the explosion blew off a panel of the service module's outer wall.

Inside the capsule, the crew felt the shudder and saw warning lights flicker. Swigert reported the now-famous line, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it for the ground. Within minutes, instruments showed that one oxygen tank was empty and the other was leaking. The fuel cells that made electricity and water from oxygen and hydrogen began to die, and the main bus voltage dropped. Looking out the window, Lovell saw gas streaming into space. "We are venting something," he told Houston. It was the spacecraft's lifeblood.

In Mission Control, flight director Gene Kranz and his team worked to understand what the instruments were saying. At first they suspected faulty sensors. Within an hour it was clear that the service module could no longer be relied on. The Moon landing was gone. The only question was whether the crew could be brought home alive.

The solution was to use the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius was designed to support two men for about two days on the Moon's surface. Now it had to keep three alive for four. The crew powered down Odyssey to save its remaining battery power for reentry, and crowded into the little lander. Mission Control ran the numbers on every resource, and every one was tight.

The first problem was trajectory. Apollo 13 was on a "free return" path that would swing around the Moon and fall back toward Earth, but it had been adjusted to aim for the landing site and would miss the planet. Controllers decided to fire Aquarius's descent engine, designed for landing, to speed up the return. Burns were made after passing the far side of the Moon, shortening the trip and aiming it for a Pacific splashdown. The crew aligned the spacecraft without its usual guidance computer, using the Earth's terminator as a reference.

Then came the cold. With almost no power, the cabin temperature dropped to near freezing. Condensation dripped from the walls. Water was rationed to a few ounces per person each day, and the crew grew dehydrated; Haise developed a kidney infection. They slept little. Lovell later recalled the discomfort, but the crew kept working.

The most dangerous problem was carbon dioxide. The lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrubbed exhaled carbon dioxide from the air, were rated for two men and began to saturate. The command module had plenty of canisters, but they were square, and the lunar module's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the same items the crew had aboard: plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a suit hose and duct tape. They devised an adapter and read the instructions up to the crew over the radio. Lovell, Haise and Swigert built it, and carbon dioxide levels dropped. It remains among the most celebrated improvisations in spaceflight.

Another difficulty lay ahead. Odyssey had to be restarted from a cold, dark state, using a procedure never tested in flight, and with limited battery power. Mattingly, the astronaut who had been grounded, worked in a simulator with engineers to write a startup sequence that stayed within the power budget. It was read to the crew in the final hours.

Before reentry the crew jettisoned the damaged service module. As it drifted away, they saw for the first time the extent of the harm: a whole panel was missing, and the side was scorched and torn. Lovell described it to Houston as "really a mess." Then they moved back into Odyssey, released Aquarius, which had saved them, and prepared for the plunge. The lander would burn up in the atmosphere.

Reentry brought one last tension. The blackout, when ionized air blocks radio, normally lasts about three minutes. This time it stretched longer, and the world waited. Controllers feared the heat shield might have been damaged. Then, after more than a minute of added silence, Swigert's voice came through. Parachutes opened, and Odyssey landed in the South Pacific on April 17 near the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. Millions had watched on television. All three men were alive.

An investigation board led by Edgar Cortright found the cause in the tank's design and handling, not in the crew or in chance. Changes followed: the oxygen tanks were redesigned, the thermostats rebuilt, and additional power and water reserves were added to the command module. Apollo flights resumed, and later crews reached the Moon.

Apollo 13 never touched down, yet it is remembered as one of the program's finest hours. NASA called it a "successful failure." The mission showed what a trained team could do when a plan collapsed: engineers, astronauts and controllers solved problem after problem in real time, with limited tools and no precedent. The three men came home because many people on the ground and in space refused to treat the situation as hopeless.
